Definition: A zero geometric cycle has zero geometric period and is not asserted to label a physical BPS state; the physical charge map is a separate supplied quotient.
Definition: The minimum allowed rank is K=2; a generic z outside the branch and puncture loci has exactly K sheet preimages under the finite degree-K cover.
Definition: At a branch value local sheet labels coalesce, so the regular ij-trajectory ODE is restricted to the complement of the branch locus and local branch/junction rules are stated separately.

Definition: Closed webs lift to absolute cycles; open lifts have the stated fixed endpoints. Admitted physical endpoint sectors are Gamma_0-orbits modulo ker rho, with affine mass-dimension-one central charges. Genericity quantifies over the bulk and both same-endpoint soliton sectors, including diagonal bulk copies; it does not quantify over framed z_1-to-z_2 sectors. Relative periods descend precisely when the kernel periods vanish.

The Definition explicitly assumes ACω for the imported mathematical trace chain. The compact self-adjoint spectral theorem uses the countable-union result and finite-eigenspace basis selection, and the singular-value decomposition also uses countable basis selection. The positive-square-root proof uses ACω through norm-limit compactness and the complete-and-totally-bounded compactness theorem. This is a mathematical premise, not a physical assumption, and no choice is made to construct the model-supplied sectors.

citations.quote:
For distinct sheets $i,j$, a regular **$ij$-trajectory of Wentzel–Kramers–Brillouin (WKB) phase** $\vartheta_{\rm W}\in\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z$ is a $C^1$ immersed path $z:I\to C\setminus\operatorname{Branch}(\pi)$, for an open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$, with $\dot z\ne0$ and

$$\operatorname{Im}\!\left(e^{-i\vartheta_{\rm W}}(\lambda^{(i)}-\lambda^{(j)})(\dot z)\right)=0.$$

The following **geometric seed convention** applies at every ramification order. An outgoing seed at a branch value $b\in\overline C$, including $b\in P$, is a germ of such an oriented regular $ij$-trajectory $z:(0,\epsilon)\to C\setminus\operatorname{Branch}(\pi)$ with $z(s)\to b$ as $s\downarrow0$, for which both sheet lifts extend continuously to the same ramification point over $b$. Two germs agree when their oriented sheet-labeled images agree sufficiently near that endpoint, up to increasing reparametrization. Take all such germs and extend each maximally through the regular locus. No number of seeds or finite network is assumed for a general cover. For a simple branch point, exactly two sheets ramify and their difference has local form $a(z)z^{1/2}dz$ with $a(0)\ne0$; its integral has leading order $z^{3/2}$, giving the familiar three outgoing directions with the exchanged-sheet labels included. This three-direction statement is a special case, not a restriction to simple ramification.

Starting with these maximal seed trajectories, form successive generations by adjoining, at each regular intersection of an $ij$-trajectory and a $jk$-trajectory with distinct $i,j,k$ and $\lambda^{(i)}-\lambda^{(k)}\ne0$, the maximal outgoing $ik$-trajectory through that point satisfying the same phase and positive-real orientation. The **geometric WKB network** is the union of all generations. This specifies a geometric closure convention at higher ramification as well; it does not assert that the general cover determines physical wall or soliton data.

For the cubic-differential case, use the following explicit conical specialization. Let $\varphi$ be a meromorphic cubic differential with simple zeros and poles of order at most two, and canonical cover $\lambda^3=\pi^*\varphi$. A zero or pole of order $m\in\{1,-1,-2\}$ is a conical singularity, with flat cone angle $2\pi(m+3)/3$ in the metric $|\varphi^{1/3}|$. In a local flat coordinate $u=\int\varphi^{1/3}$, the KT convention at phase $\vartheta_{\rm KT}$ seeds every outward critical ray of slope $\vartheta_{\rm KT}+n\pi/3$, $n\in\mathbb Z$, from every conical singularity, even a marked pole. Even $n$ gives positive rays and odd $n$ negative rays. Extend them maximally; at each regular intersection of two rays of the same sign, adjoin the outgoing ray of the opposite sign, and iterate. This is the conical cubic convention of Kidwai and Tahar, not a simple-branch approximation. For sheets $\lambda^{(j)}=\omega\lambda^{(i)}$, $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$, their difference is $(1-\omega)\lambda^{(i)}$ with $\arg(1-\omega)=-\pi/6$. Thus the unlabelled seed supports agree with the sheet-pair convention when $\vartheta_{\rm W}=\vartheta_{\rm KT}-\pi/6$ modulo $\pi/3$; the ordered pair and orientation fix the exact phase. For T3, the cover is fully ramified over its three double poles and $\lambda$ is nonzero at the corresponding cover points. In its flat cover coordinate there are six outgoing rays with angles $\vartheta_{\rm KT}+n\pi/3$ at each such point, projected to the base. No soliton index is assigned by this conical rule.

A **finite web** is a finite connected metric ribbon graph: each edge has positive finite length and a cyclic order at each vertex; each internal vertex is trivalent and maps to a network joint, and each external univalent vertex maps to a branch point.

The physical charge group $\Gamma_{\mathcal T}$ is a model-specified quotient of a subgroup $\Gamma_0\le\Gamma_{\rm geom}$, supplied with a surjective quotient map $\rho:\Gamma_0\to\Gamma_{\mathcal T}$; it is not identified with all of $H_1(\widetilde\Sigma;\mathbb Z)$ by notation alone.

derivations.claim: On the affine curve $y^3=x(x-1)$, $dx/y^2$ cubes to the specified differential. There are exactly three fully ramified points, over $0,1,\infty$. Near the first two, use $y$ as a coordinate: differentiation gives $dx/y^2=3\,dy/(2x-1)$, which extends holomorphically and is nonzero. Near infinity take a parameter $t$ with $x=t^{-3}$ and $y=t^{-2}h(t)$, where $h(t)^3=1-t^3$ and $h(0)=1$; then $dx/y^2=-3h(t)^{-2}dt$, again holomorphic and nonzero. Away from these points the cover is unramified and the form is nonzero. Along the lift $q$ of $[0,1]$ with $y=-[x(1-x)]^{1/3}$ the form is positive real, and $\int_q\lambda_{\rm geom}=\beta$. The integral converges because both endpoint exponents are $-2/3>-1$. The three oriented lifts are $q,\tau q,\tau^2q$, and their integrals are $\beta,\omega\beta,\omega^2\beta$.

The inverse image $G=\pi^{-1}([0,1])$ is a graph with two vertices and these three edges. Its complement is one open disk: $\mathbb P^1\setminus[0,1]$ is an open disk containing the single remaining branch value $\infty$, and its punctured-disk cover is connected with cyclic monodromy of order three; cutting along a radius gives three slit disks glued cyclically, whose missing central point fills to one disk by the local degree-three model. Thus the compact surface has a cell decomposition with $G$ as its one-skeleton and one two-cell. The oriented attaching boundary traverses each graph edge once in each direction, so its cellular boundary is zero. The integral cycle group of $G$ consists of the triples $(n_0,n_1,n_2)$ with $n_0+n_1+n_2=0$; a basis is $(1,-1,0),(0,1,-1)$. Consequently $[q-\tau q]$ and $[\tau q-\tau^2q]$ form a basis of $H_1(\Sigma;\mathbb Z)$, and the full period group is $a(\mathbb Z+\omega\mathbb Z)$, with $a=(1-\omega)\beta$. Integration is unchanged by homotopy or a boundary: subdivide a homotopy or singular two-simplex into finitely many pieces contained in primitive disks, then the primitive endpoint differences cancel on internal edges. This also justifies using the cellular cycle representatives to compute all periods.

Define $f:\Sigma\to\mathbb C/(a\mathbb Z+a\omega\mathbb Z)$ by integration from $\widetilde A$ modulo the period group. Step 2.1 makes this well-defined, and its derivative is the nowhere-zero form from step 1.1, so it is a local biholomorphism. Compactness makes its image closed; local invertibility makes it open, so connectedness of the target makes it surjective and a finite covering. The two loops in step 2.1 map to the two target lattice generators; hence the induced fundamental-group image is the entire target group $\mathbb Z^2$. A connected covering with this image has one sheet: lifting target loops permutes its fiber transitively, whereas loops in the image fix the chosen point, so surjectivity leaves only that point. Thus $f$ is a biholomorphism. Dividing its coordinate by $a$ gives the asserted $w$ and $\lambda_{\rm geom}=a\,dw$. Along $q$, $w$ runs straight from $0$ to $\beta/a=1/(1-\omega)=(2+\omega)/3$, so constant flat-speed parametrization is exactly $p(t)=[t(2+\omega)/3]$. Integration also gives $w(\tau P)=\omega w(P)$. The fixed classes of this rotation solve $(1-\omega)w\in\mathbb Z+\omega\mathbb Z$; the determinant of multiplication by $1-\omega$ is $3$, and the three distinct solutions are the displayed $\widetilde A,\widetilde B,\widetilde C$. The remaining branch point therefore has the asserted coordinate $\widetilde C$.

The displacement $(2+\omega)/3=1/2+i\sqrt3/6$ has unit-coordinate length $1/\sqrt3$ and coordinate angle $\vartheta_w=\pi/6$. Since $a=(1-\omega)\beta=\sqrt3\beta e^{-i\pi/6}$, its actual flat length is $|a|/\sqrt3=\beta$ and its actual geometric phase is $\vartheta_{\rm KT}=0$. The ordered sheet difference $(1-\omega)\lambda_{\rm geom}$ along this path has phase $\vartheta_{\rm W}=-\pi/6$, with positive real part after multiplication by $e^{i\pi/6}$. The coordinate-slope formula has coprime $(p_0,q_0)=(2,1)$ and determinant $4-2+1=3$; the rotation from $w$ to the flat coordinate must be included when interpreting this as a network phase. Finally, $\int_p\lambda_{\rm geom}=a(2+\omega)/3=\beta$.

A point on the open segment has basis coordinates $(2s/3,s/3)$ for $0<s<1$. It cannot equal a lattice translate of $\widetilde A$, since that would require an integer second coordinate $s/3\in(0,1/3)$; it cannot equal a translate of $\widetilde B$, since the second coordinate would require $s=1+3n$ for an integer $n$, which has no solution in $(0,1)$; and it cannot equal a translate of $\widetilde C$, since it would require $s=2+3n$, also with no solution in $(0,1)$. Thus the open segment contains no branch point. It is embedded on the torus since a nonzero difference between two points on it has norm less than $1/\sqrt3$, whereas every nonzero lattice vector has norm at least $1$. Its projection under $\pi$ also has no interior self-identification: for $0<s,t<1$, the basis coordinates of $p(t)-\tau(p(s))$ are $((2t+s)/3,(t-s)/3)$, which cannot both be integers, and those of $p(t)-\tau^2(p(s))$ are $((2t+s)/3,(t+2s)/3)\in(0,1)^2$, also not a lattice vector. Therefore the projected path is an embedded regular trajectory from one conical branch value to the other. At each endpoint the lifts $p$ and $\tau(p)$ end at the same fully ramified point, so their outgoing ordered-pair germ is a seed by [F2], even though its branch value is a marked double pole. Equivalently, $\lambda_{\rm geom}$ is nonzero there by step 1.1, and the outgoing cover ray is one of the KT conical rays at $\vartheta_{\rm KT}=0$; reversing direction exchanges the sheet labels and gives the corresponding outgoing ray from the other endpoint. The maximal extensions therefore contain this segment from both endpoints, in both orientations; these orientations form a double wall.

The graph $T=[0,1]$ with its single edge assigned length $\beta$ in the KT cover metric is finite and connected, has two univalent external vertices and no internal vertices, and maps isometrically to the projected double wall because $\pi$ is an unramified local isometry on its open edge. In the GMN sheet-difference metric its edge length is $|1-\omega|\beta=\sqrt3\,\beta=c$, whose GMN-normalized value is $c/\pi$ in the source's geometric units; no physical mass is asserted. Thus it satisfies the finite-web definition in either explicitly declared convention.

On the interior of the projected web, the two lifts $p$ and $\tau(p)$ are distinct sheets because the only deck fixed points are the three branch points excluded in step 5.1. If $s_i,s_j$ are these sheet sections over that interval, $s_i^*\lambda_{\rm geom}-s_j^*\lambda_{\rm geom}=(1-\omega)s_i^*\lambda_{\rm geom}$, by $\tau^*\lambda_{\rm geom}=\omega\lambda_{\rm geom}$. These are exactly the ordered sheet labels used in step 4.1, with constant sheet-difference phase $-\pi/6$. At each endpoint all three sheets coalesce, so the forward $i$ lift and reversed $j$ lift join continuously; the chosen sheet-lift rule of [F4] therefore assigns this very web the closed chain $p-\tau(p)$. Its period is $\int_{p-\tau(p)}\lambda_{\rm geom}=(1-\omega)\int_p\lambda_{\rm geom}=(1-\omega)\beta=a=ce^{-i\pi/6}\ne0$. In the unit-lattice coordinate the displacement of this cycle is $(1-\omega)(2+\omega)/3=1$, agreeing with this period. It is a primitive nonzero homology class by the basis computation in step 2.1; independently, its nonzero period excludes a boundary by the primitive-disk argument there. Its phase $-\pi/6$ is congruent to $\vartheta_{\rm KT}+\pi/2=\pi/2$ modulo $\pi/3$; this congruence is only a phase check and does not identify our sheet-pair lift with the source's canonical KT lift. The chain construction, rather than that congruence, establishes the web–cycle relation. This proves the web's nonzero geometric class and exact period under the declared lift rule, not an unconditional physical identification.

Under the assumptions of [A1], the descended physical central charge is $Z_{\mathcal T}(\rho(\gamma_{\rm geom}))=\pi^{-1}\int_{\gamma_{\rm geom}}m_*\lambda_{\rm geom}=m_*a/\pi\ne0$. Since $Z_{\mathcal T}$ is additive, it sends zero to zero, so $\rho(\gamma_{\rm geom})\ne0$. Without the assumptions in [A1], no physical charge image follows.
